author: Minucius Felix
addressee: The dialogue is addressed to the reader, framed as the author's recollection of a debate among friends; the internal audience is Marcus, the narrator.
occasion: Minucius Felix recalls a visit to Ostia with his friends Octavius and Caecilius. When Caecilius, a pagan, kisses a statue of Serapis, Octavius reproaches him, and Caecilius proposes a formal debate about pagan religion and Christianity, with the author as judge.
argument: Caecilius first argues that human knowledge is uncertain, that Rome owes its greatness to traditional worship of the gods, and that Christians are a depraved secret society deserving punishment. Octavius replies that the order of the universe proves one creator God, that the pagan gods were merely deified humans and their myths are immoral, and that demons inspire pagan oracles and slanders against Christians. He defends Christian morals, worship, and hope of resurrection, and argues that Christian endurance under suffering shows God's power. Caecilius concedes defeat, acknowledges providence and the Christian God, and the friends depart joyfully.

outline.move: The narrator fondly remembers his friend Octavius and describes the trip to Ostia that led to the debate.
Caecilius kisses a statue of Serapis, Octavius rebukes him, and the friends sit down by the sea to hold a formal debate.
Caecilius argues that human knowledge is uncertain, that traditional Roman religion deserves reverence, and that Rome's power proves the gods' favor.
Caecilius attacks Christians as a secret, criminal sect with absurd beliefs about one hidden God, resurrection, and judgment, and urges them to follow Socrates' humble doubt.
The narrator, as judge, urges both sides to weigh truth rather than eloquence; Caecilius objects that the interruption weakens his case, and the narrator allows Octavius to reply.
Octavius argues that the order of the universe proves one creator God, and that philosophers and poets actually agree on one divine mind.
Octavius shows that the pagan gods were deified humans, that their myths and rites are immoral or ridiculous, and that Roman power came from crime, not piety.
Octavius explains that demons inspire pagan oracles and slanders against Christians, and that Christians themselves once believed such lies before examining them.
Octavius refutes the charges of worshiping a crucified criminal, killing infants, and practicing incest, turning the accusations back on pagan rites.
Octavius explains Christian worship, providence, resurrection, judgment, poverty, and endurance, and contrasts Christian purity with pagan immorality.
Caecilius admits he is defeated, acknowledges providence and the Christian God, and the friends part joyfully.

cast.name: Marcus Minucius Felix
cast.who: The narrator and author, a lawyer and friend of Octavius and Caecilius, who acts as judge of the debate.

cast.name: Octavius
cast.who: A Christian friend of the narrator, now deceased, who defends Christianity in the debate.

cast.name: Caecilius
cast.who: A pagan friend who attacks Christianity and defends traditional Roman religion, and is converted at the end.

voices.speaker: Caecilius
voices.how_marked: Introduced by narrative phrases such as 'Caecilius exorsus est' and 'inquit Caecilius'.

voices.speaker: Octavius
voices.how_marked: Introduced by narrative phrases such as 'Et Octauius' and 'inquit Octauius'.

voices.speaker: Marcus (the narrator)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by narrative phrases such as 'inquam' and 'cui ego'.

key_terms.sense: False or excessive religious practice, especially pagan worship and fear of the gods.
Proper worship and reverence, either true religion or traditional Roman cult.
Impure spirits that deceive humans through idols, oracles, and slanders against Christians.
God's ordering and care of the universe, which Caecilius doubts and Octavius defends.
Blind chance or destiny, which Caecilius invokes and Octavius redefines as God's decree.
The Christian hope of bodily restoration after death, mocked by Caecilius and defended by Octavius.
An idol or image of a pagan god, which Octavius argues is lifeless matter.
Divine power or deity, often used of the pagan gods.
True wisdom, which Octavius says is available to all people through reason, not only to philosophers.
The truth about God and religion, which the debate seeks to establish.
The alleged sexual immorality of Christians, which Octavius refutes and turns back on pagan myths and practices.
Impiety or violation of what is sacred, used both of Christian alleged crimes and pagan worship of captured gods.
Spirit, used both of God's nature and of the impure spirits that deceive humans.
Mind or reason, identified by Octavius with God's nature and with the human capacity to know God.
Reason or rational order, both in the universe and in human understanding of God.

uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain; it is placed in the late second or early third century AD.
The precise identity of the author beyond his name is uncertain.
Whether the dialogue records a real event or is a literary fiction is uncertain.

_unresolved_facts.claim: When Caecilius, a pagan, kisses a statue of Serapis, Octavius reproaches him
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Caecilius simulacro Serapidis denotato, ut uulgus superstitiosus solet, manum ori admouens osculum labiis inpressit. / Tunc Octauius ait: Non boni uiri est, Marce frater, hominem domi forisque lateri tuo inhaerentem sic in hac inperitiae uulgaris caecitate deserere, ut tam luculento die in lapides eum patiaris inpingere
_unresolved_facts.fix: Octavius reproaches Marcus (the narrator), not Caecilius, for allowing his friend Caecilius to persist in superstition without intervention

_unresolved_facts.claim: Caecilius proposes a formal debate about pagan religion and Christianity
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: tum ille: Iam dudum me Octaui nostri acriter angit et remordet oratio, qua in te inuectus obiurgauit neglegentiae, ut me dissimulanter grauius argueret inscientiae.. itaque progrediar ulterius: de toto et integro mihi cum Octauio res est. si placet, ut ipsius sectae homo cum eo disputem
_unresolved_facts.fix: Caecilius proposes to debate with Octavius as a fellow-member of his own sect (ut ipsius sectae homo), not as a pagan defending pagan religion against Christianity

_unresolved_facts.claim: Caecilius first argues that human knowledge is uncertain, that Rome owes its greatness to traditional worship of the gods, and that Christians are a depraved secret society deserving punishment
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: eruenda prorsus haec et execranda consensio
_unresolved_facts.fix: Caecilius argues that human knowledge is uncertain (section 5), that traditional Roman religion deserves reverence and Rome owes its power to religious observance (sections 6-7), and that Christians are a secret criminal conspiracy deserving extermination (sections 8-9); he does not explicitly call for 'punishment' but for eradication ('eruenda')

_unresolved_facts.claim: Octavius replies that the order of the universe proves one creator God, that the pagan gods were merely deified humans and their myths are immoral, and that demons inspire pagan oracles and slanders against Christians
sections 5, 6, 7: 'Caecilius argues that human knowledge is uncertain, that traditional Roman religion deserves reverence, and that Rome's power proves the gods' favor'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ita quicquid Romani tenent, colunt, possident, audaciae praeda est: templa omnia de manubiis, id est de ruinis urbium, de spoliis deorum, de caedibus sacerdotum
_unresolved_facts.fix: In sections 5-7, Caecilius argues that human knowledge is uncertain (5), that ancestral Roman religion should be preserved (6), and that Rome's power proves the gods' favor (6-7). However, the brief's outline for sections 21-25 more accurately captures Octavius's counter-argument that Roman power came from crime, not piety

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections 21, 22, 23, 24, 25: 'Octavius shows that the pagan gods were deified humans, that their myths and rites are immoral or ridiculous, and that Roman power came from crime, not piety'
sections 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38: 'Octavius explains Christian worship, providence, resurrection, judgment, poverty, and endurance, and contrasts Christian purity with pagan immorality'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: sed Iudaeis nihil profuit, quod unum et ipsi Deum aris atque templis maxima superstitione coluerunt
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 33 is largely a digression on Jewish history and their fall from God's favor, not directly about 'Christian worship, providence, resurrection, judgment, poverty, and endurance'. The brief's characterization elides the specific anti-Jewish polemic in this section

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Cogitanti mihi et cum animo meo Octaui boni et fidelissimi contubernalis memoriam recensenti
_unresolved_facts.fix: The narrator is never named as 'Minucius Felix' in the text; he is addressed as 'Marce frater' by Octavius (section 3) and 'Marce frater' by Caecilius (section 5). The identification with Marcus Minucius Felix is external scholarly inference, not a source form

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Sic Caecilius et renidens (nam indignationis eius tumorem effusae orationis impetus relaxauerat): Ecquid ad haec, ait, audet Octauius
_unresolved_facts.fix: Caecilius also speaks in section 14 (opening with 'Sic Caecilius et renidens... Ecquid ad haec, ait, audet Octauius') and section 40 ('Ego Octauio meo plurimum quantum...'). The brief omits these sections from Caecilius's voice
The narrator Marcus speaks in section 14 ('Parce, inquam, in eum plaudere'), not Octavius. The brief incorrectly attributes this to Octavius or omits it from Marcus's sections

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Cogitanti mihi et cum animo meo Octaui boni et fidelissimi contubernalis memoriam recensenti
_unresolved_facts.fix: Marcus the narrator speaks throughout the framing narrative in sections 1-4, not just section 4. The brief underrepresents the narrator's voice in the opening sections
